focus: Teach Einstein's spherical-particle diffusion and the root-mean-square displacement along ONE axis. Use four editable scalar sliders: absolute temperature T in K (250-400, default 300); dynamic viscosity eta in mPa*s (0.1-5, default 1); particle RADIUS a in micrometres (0.1-5, default 1); elapsed time t in seconds (0-60, default 1). Compute D in micrometres squared per second as 0.01380649*T/(6*3.141592653589793*eta*a). Then compute mean-square displacement MSD = 2*D*t and one-axis RMS = sqrt(2*D*t), showing all three quantities with units. The decimal coefficient and pi approximation are modern teaching/unit conversions, not numbers fitted by Einstein. Explain that quadrupling time doubles RMS, doubling viscosity or radius halves D, and t=0 gives zero MSD and RMS while D stays positive. Use a line view sweeping t for RMS. Do not present a deterministic particle trajectory or confuse RMS with mean signed displacement, mean absolute displacement, path length, or 3D RMS. All entered values are teaching examples rather than reproduction of measurements.
excerpt:
On the Movement of Small Particles Suspended in a Stationary Liquid Demanded by the Molecular-Kinetic Theory of Heat (1905), A. D. Cowper translation. Section 3, printed page 12, and Section 4, equation (11), printed page 17 (PDF pages 8 and 10).
Prose excerpt: The mean displacement is therefore proportional to the square root of the time.
Equation transcription from Section 3: D = (R*T/N)/(6*pi*k*P), where k is the liquid's viscosity coefficient and P is the sphere's radius.
Equation transcription from Section 4, equation (11): lambda_x = sqrt(mean(x^2)) = sqrt(2*D*t). The preceding passage identifies this quantity as the square root of the arithmetic mean of squared displacements along the x-axis.
Teaching notation and SI conversion: write eta for viscosity and a for radius, and use k_B = R/N. Modern exact k_B = 1.380649e-23 J/K is supplied from NIST, https://www.nist.gov/si-redefinition/kelvin/kelvin-boltzmann-constant; this numerical value is not quoted from the 1905 paper. With eta in mPa*s, a in micrometres, and D in micrometres squared per second, D = 0.01380649*T/(6*pi*eta*a). The factors 1e-3 Pa*s per mPa*s, 1e-6 metres per micrometre and 1e12 square micrometres per square metre give this converted coefficient.
